```lua
        part:Destroy()
    end
end)
```

answer_key: Touched fires repeatedly/multiple times in quick succession (once per touching body part / physics contact), so the handler runs several times
Fix: add a debounce/cooldown or 'already collected' flag checked and set at the top of the handler before awarding (per-part flag, or per-player timestamp table)

```lua
  if taken then return end
  local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
  if not plr then return end
  local hum = hit.Parent:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
```

A LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts does:
```lua
local door = workspace.Map.Buildings.Hotel.Door
door.Touched:Connect(onTouch)
```
In a large map players report 'Door is not a valid member of Model' errors, mostly for doors far from spawn. StreamingEnabled is on. Diagnose and give two valid fixes.
answer_key: Cause: with StreamingEnabled, instances outside the streaming radius are not replicated to the client yet (or have streamed out), so the path does not exist when the script runs
Fix 1: use WaitForChild (or ChildAdded / CollectionService added signal) rather than direct indexing, and tolerate parts streaming in/out

Fix 2: set the model's ModelStreamingMode to Atomic (WaitForChild the model) or Persistent (wait for Workspace.PersistentLoaded), or move the logic to a server script; Persistent should be used sparingly

responses.R1:
With StreamingEnabled the client only has instances near the player; far doors (or ancestors like Hotel) aren't streamed in yet, and can stream out later, so direct indexing at startup throws. Fix 1: wait for it: `local hotel = workspace.Map.Buildings:WaitForChild("Hotel", 10)` then `hotel and hotel:WaitForChild("Door", 10)`, handle nil, and set the Hotel model's ModelStreamingMode = Atomic so it arrives whole (or Persistent if it must always exist, at a memory cost). Fix 2 (better): tag doors with CollectionService and bind as they stream in/out:
```lua
local CS = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local conns = {}
local function add(d) if not conns[d] then conns[d] = d.Touched:Connect(onTouch) end end
CS:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door"):Connect(add)
CS:GetInstanceRemovedSignal("Door"):Connect(function(d)
	if conns[d] then conns[d]:Disconnect() conns[d] = nil end
end)
for _, d in CS:GetTagged("Door") do add(d) end
```
Also consider handling gameplay door touches on the server, where everything exists. Don't fix it by turning streaming off.
responses.R2: With StreamingEnabled the client only has the instances near the player. Distant parts of the map (the Hotel door) are not streamed in yet when the LocalScript runs, or they get streamed out later. Direct dot-indexing errors when the child isn't present. Fix 1: wait for it, with a timeout: local door = workspace:WaitForChild('Map'):WaitForChild('Buildings'):WaitForChild('Hotel'):WaitForChild('Door', 10), and handle nil plus later stream-out (door.AncestryChanged / Destroying). Fix 2 (better): tag doors with CollectionService and use GetInstanceAddedSignal('Door') plus GetTagged, connecting Touched when each door streams in and cleaning up on InstanceRemoved. Alternatives: set the Hotel model's ModelStreamingMode = Atomic or Persistent (Persistent keeps it always loaded, so use it sparingly), or handle door touches on the server, where everything exists.
responses.R3: With StreamingEnabled the client only has parts near the player; far doors haven't streamed in when the LocalScript runs, so indexing `Hotel.Door` errors (and they can stream out later). Fix 1: wait for it: `local door = workspace.Map.Buildings.Hotel:WaitForChild("Door")` (with the whole path using WaitForChild, optionally with timeout, and handle it streaming out/being replaced). Fix 2 (better for many doors): tag doors with CollectionService and use `CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door")` plus `GetTagged`, connecting Touched when each door streams in and disconnecting on GetInstanceRemovedSignal. Alternatively set the Hotel model's ModelStreamingMode = Persistent (always sent to clients) or Atomic, or handle door touches on the server.

With StreamingEnabled, the client only has instances near the player. Distant buildings and their doors aren't streamed in yet, so indexing workspace.Map.Buildings.Hotel.Door throws "not a valid member". The parts can also stream out later, so the reference becomes invalid.
Fixes:
1. Make the model persistent or atomic: set Hotel (or the Door model) ModelStreamingMode = Persistent, so it is always present on clients (use sparingly). Or set Atomic and wait for it with WaitForChild.
2. Don't assume it exists. Use CollectionService tags: tag doors "Door", then use GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door") and GetTagged to connect when a door streams in, and clean up on GetInstanceRemovedSignal. ```lua

```lua
local door = hotel:WaitForChild("Door") -- may wait until in range (no timeout = may yield indefinitely)
```
Better, tag doors with CollectionService and use GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door") plus GetTagged. Connect when a door streams in and clean up on GetInstanceRemovedSignal. That covers stream-in, stream-out and new doors.
Fix 2 (keep it loaded): make the door model always present on clients. Put it in a Model with ModelStreamingMode = Persistent (or Atomic for all-or-nothing loading), or call player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(position) before using it.
Also consider moving Touched handling for doors to the server, which always has every part, and replicating the result.

Players report that after buying a developer product they were sometimes charged but received nothing, and sometimes received double coins. Code:
```lua
local MPS = game:GetService('MarketplaceService')
MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
    local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
    local ok = pcall(function()
        store:SetAsync(plr.UserId, (store:GetAsync(plr.UserId) or 0) + 100)
    end)
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```
List the bugs and the corrected behavior.
answer_key: Returns PurchaseGranted unconditionally: if the DataStore call fails (ok == false) or the player has left (plr is nil), it must return NotProcessedYet so the receipt is retried
Not idempotent: receipts can be re-delivered, so record info.PurchaseId and skip the grant if already processed (ideally inside one UpdateAsync)
Uses non-atomic Get+Set instead of UpdateAsync, and plr is not nil-checked (errors when the player left)

responses.R1: Bugs: (1) plr can be nil if the player left; plr.UserId errors inside pcall, so ok = false. (2) The pcall result is ignored: it returns PurchaseGranted even when the save failed -> charged, nothing received. (3) No PurchaseId dedupe -> Roblox retries the receipt (timeout, rejoin, another server) and coins are added twice. (4) GetAsync + SetAsync is a non-atomic read-modify-write; use UpdateAsync. (5) Coins don't update the live session data, and it ignores ProductId. Corrected: if player missing -> NotProcessedYet; route by info.ProductId; in one UpdateAsync on the player's profile, check a stored processed-receipt list for info.PurchaseId, if absent add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId (cap list size); only if the update succeeds return PurchaseGranted (also if already recorded); any error -> NotProcessedYet. Update the in-memory/leaderstats value after success. Assign ProcessReceipt only once.
responses.R2:
Bugs:
1. It always returns PurchaseGranted, even if pcall failed. So when the save errors, the receipt is closed and the player is charged but gets nothing.
2. It ignores a player who isn't present. If plr is nil, plr.UserId errors inside the pcall, so nothing is saved, but it still returns Granted.
3. There is no idempotency. Roblox retries receipts (timeout, rejoin, server crash after the save but before the return), and each retry adds 100 again, giving double coins. There is no PurchaseId record.
4. GetAsync + SetAsync is a non-atomic read-modify-write. Another server or autosave can race and overwrite.
5. It probably doesn't update the in-memory session data, so the next autosave overwrites the purchase.
Corrected behaviour: look up the player, and return NotProcessedYet if they are absent. In one UpdateAsync on the player's key, if receipts[PurchaseId] already exists, change nothing; otherwise add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId. Return Granted only if pcall succeeded; on any error, return NotProcessedYet. Then update the live session or leaderstats. Check ProductId, and keep a single ProcessReceipt assignment.

```lua
local function safeTeleport(placeId: number, players: {Player}, teleportData: any?)
    local options = Instance.new("TeleportOptions")
    if teleportData ~= nil then options:SetTeleportData(teleportData) end
```

Persistent progress (coins, loadout) belongs in DataStores (keyed by UserId) loaded by the destination server; MemoryStores for short-lived cross-server state

Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData, read with GetJoinData or GetLocalPlayerTeleportData) goes through the client. prompt: You are building a racing game with drivable cars. Decide who should have network ownership of the car, what the security risk is, and what the server must still validate.
answer_key: The driver's client should own the car for responsive physics (SetNetworkOwner on the server when seated; release to automatic when empty); the server always owns anchored parts
Client ownership means Roblox cannot verify the physics: exploiters can teleport parts or move them through walls, and Touched events on owned parts can be fired by that client
Server must validate critical outcomes (checkpoints, lap times, speed/position plausibility, damage); use SetNetworkOwner(nil) for gameplay-critical parts
Use ownership changes sparingly because they can cause jitter

responses.R1: Give network ownership of the car's assembly to the driver: on seat occupancy, call vehicle.PrimaryPart:SetNetworkOwner(player) on the server (and SetNetworkOwner(nil) or automatic when they leave). That gives responsive, lag-free physics for the driver, and server ownership would feel laggy. The risk: the owning client simulates the physics and the server accepts it, so an exploiter can teleport the car, speed-hack, fly, noclip, or fling other players and parts it touches. The server must still validate: speed and acceleration caps and position deltas between frames (teleport detection, with a rubber band or reclaiming ownership if exceeded); checkpoint order and lap or finish times (detect checkpoints on the server, enforce minimum plausible times); that the car stays in bounds and isn't flying; that only the seated driver can own or control it; and all rewards and results on the server. Don't trust remote-reported positions or times. Never give ownership of unanchored world parts unnecessarily.

Ownership: give the driver's client network ownership of the car (VehicleSeat.Occupant changed: car.PrimaryPart:SetNetworkOwner(player); on exit, return it to the server or nil). Risk: the owner simulates the car's physics, and the server accepts whatever position and velocity they report. An exploiter can teleport, speed-hack, fly, fling other players with their car, or noclip, and the server sees it as legitimate physics.
The server must still validate:
- Sanity checks on position deltas and speed against the car's max speed (per heartbeat). Use checkpoint and lap order with timing (no skipping, minimum lap time). Out-of-bounds or under-map checks, and teleport detection. Reset or revoke ownership (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) or flag the player on a violation.
- All game outcomes: lap counting, finish times, rewards and collisions that damage others are decided on the server, never from client remotes.

prompt: A shooter sends each player's aim direction and position to the server 30 times per second via a RemoteEvent, causing bandwidth and queue pressure. Recommend a better transport and describe its constraints and how to handle them.
answer_key: Use UnreliableRemoteEvent for frequent, ephemeral state where the latest value matters
Payloads over 1,000 bytes may be dropped, so keep messages small
Messages can be dropped or arrive out of order and are dropped when no handler is connected: include a sequence number/timestamp and ignore stale ones
Keep important one-off events (damage, purchases) on reliable RemoteEvents

Handling: send only on change, throttled to ~10-20 Hz; keep payloads small (pitch/yaw numbers or packed buffer rather than CFrames); include a sequence number/timestamp and ignore stale packets; interpolate on receivers; keep important events (fire, hit claims, reload) on reliable RemoteEvents; validate and rate-limit on the server. Position already replicates via character physics, so don't send it.

- Delivery is unordered and lossy. Send absolute state (not deltas), include a sequence number or timestamp, and drop older packets on the receiver.

- Reduce the rate. Send at 10-20 Hz or only when aim changes beyond a threshold, and interpolate on receivers. The character position already replicates through physics, so don't resend it. Batch multiple values into one event.
- Validate and rate-limit on the server like any remote (types, NaN, max rate, plausible angles).
- Rebroadcast to other clients, also unreliably, ideally only to nearby players.

prompt: Server frame time spikes because 200 NPCs each do several raycasts and path scoring every Heartbeat on the main thread. How would you use Parallel Luau for this, and what limitations must you design around?
answer_key: Split NPC logic across multiple Actors (scripts under one Actor run serially, so parallelism needs several Actors)
Use task.desynchronize() (or ConnectParallel) for the heavy read/compute work such as raycasts, then task.synchronize() before modifying the data model
Most property writes/functions are unsafe in parallel so results are applied in a serial phase; require() cannot be called in a desynchronized phase
Use SendMessage/BindToMessageParallel or SharedTable for cross-Actor data; avoid long unyielding computations

responses.R1:
Use Parallel Luau with Actors. Put the NPCs (or batches of them, for example 8-20 Actors each owning a group) under Actor instances, each with its own Script. In each Actor, connect RunService.Heartbeat with ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize()) to do the read-only, heavy work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe), distance and path scoring, target selection. Then call task.synchronize() and apply the results serially: set CFrames or Humanoid:MoveTo, change properties, fire remotes.
Limitations to design around:
- In the parallel phase you can read most instances but cannot write most properties, create or destroy instances, or call many non-thread-safe APIs (check each API's thread safety). Writes happen only after synchronize, where they are serial again.
- Actors don't share Luau state: no shared tables or module state across Actors. Communicate with Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage or SharedTable (which costs synchronization). Each Actor's require gets its own module copy.
- Parallel work is worth it only for chunky work. Per-NPC actors with tiny jobs add overhead, so batch them. Schedule spreading (not every NPC every frame, staggered updates) often gives more.
- PathfindingService:ComputeAsync yields and isn't a parallel tool; compute paths less often.
- The thread count depends on the server's cores. Profile with the MicroProfiler.
responses.R2: Split the NPCs across Actors. Put each NPC (or a batch of about 10-25) under an Actor with its own Script. In that script, connect RunService.Heartbeat with ConnectParallel (or call task.desynchronize()) to run the raycasts and path scoring in parallel. Raycasts and spatial queries are safe in parallel. Write results into actor-local tables, then call task.synchronize() (or use SharedTable or messages) to apply changes such as setting CFrames, Humanoid:MoveTo, or firing events in the serial phase. Limitations: in the parallel phase most instance writes (property sets, creating or destroying instances) are disallowed and only thread-safe APIs work. Scripts in different Actors don't share Lua state, so communicate through Actor:SendMessage, BindToMessageParallel or SharedTable (copying costs). PathfindingService:ComputeAsync is not parallel-safe and yields, so run pathing less often (stagger it, cache paths) in serial or a few per frame. Keep each actor's work coarse, not one actor per tiny task, because there is scheduling and sync overhead. Measure in the MicroProfiler. prompt: Your game autosaves every player's data with SetAsync every 5 seconds. With 80 players you see DataStore queue warnings and sometimes lost saves (queue full, error code 302). Explain the cause and a better design.
answer_key: Requests are throttled by per-server and per-experience budgets that scale with player count; exceeding them queues requests, and a full queue (30 requests) drops them with codes such as 302 for SetAsync
Reduce frequency (autosave every few minutes, staggered), save only changed data, and combine fields into one key rather than many keys

Better: keep data in a session cache, mark it dirty on change, autosave every 60-300s per player with staggered/jittered offsets, only if dirty; use UpdateAsync with session locking (or ProfileStore); save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose; retry with exponential backoff and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before writing; keep profiles small.

Writing the same key every 5 s also hits per-key throughput limits. Better: keep data in a server-side session cache; autosave each player every 60-300 s, staggered across the interval, and only when dirty; save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose; use UpdateAsync with a session lock instead of SetAsync; pcall with exponential backoff; check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType and defer non-critical saves when low; one combined key per player. ProfileStore implements this.
responses.R3:

Each key also allows only about 1 write per 6 seconds, so writing the same key every 5 seconds exceeds the per-key limit. Requests pile up in the throttle queue; once the queue is full (error 302, "request dropped, queue full"), saves are dropped and lost. SetAsync also blindly overwrites.

- Keep data in a server-side session cache and mark it dirty on change.
- Autosave every 60-120 seconds (or longer), staggered across players (each on its own offset), and only if dirty.

prompt: Describe Roblox's Input Action System: its three core instance types, how an action signals a press, and how a menu context is made to take precedence over the default player scripts.
answer_key: Core instances: InputContext (group of actions; Enabled and Priority), InputAction (has a Type such as Bool/Direction1D/2D/3D/ViewportPosition), InputBinding (maps hardware input to an action)
Bool actions fire Pressed and Released; StateChanged fires for all action types
Higher context Priority processes input first; enabling Sink consumes bound KeyCodes and blocks lower-priority contexts
Enabled per project with the Workspace property PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem

responses.R1: The Input Action System has three core instances. InputContext is a group of actions that can be enabled or disabled together, with a Priority and a Sink option. InputAction is an abstract action (for example Jump or Sprint) with a Type (Bool, Direction1D, Direction2D, ViewportPosition and so on). InputBinding sits under an action and maps a physical input to it: KeyCode (keyboard or gamepad), UIButton (a touch or GUI button), or composite directional keys (Up/Down/Left/Right). A press is signalled by the action's events: Pressed and Released for Bool actions, and StateChanged(newState) for any type, with InputAction:GetState() to poll. The action fires regardless of device, so one handler covers keyboard, gamepad and touch. Menu precedence: put the menu's actions in their own InputContext with a higher Priority than the default player scripts' (gameplay) context, and set Sink = true so inputs bound in the menu context are consumed and don't reach lower-priority contexts (character movement or jump). Enable it when the menu opens and disable it on close (InputContext.Enabled).

A Bool action signals a press through its Pressed and Released events (and StateChanged with the new value; GetState to poll). Three core instances:
- InputContext: a group of actions (a "mode", such as Gameplay, Menu or Vehicle). It has Enabled, Priority and Sink properties. It's placed somewhere the client sees it, for example under PlayerGui or in a LocalScript's tree.
- InputAction: one logical action (Jump, Sprint, Move). Its Type sets the value shape: Bool, Direction1D, Direction2D, ViewportPosition and so on.
- InputBinding: maps a physical input to its parent action. It can be a KeyCode (keyboard, gamepad or mouse button), a UIButton (a GuiButton for touch), or composite directional keys (Up/Down/Left/Right) for 2D actions, with options such as Scale and PressedThreshold.

Precedence: when the menu opens, enable a Menu InputContext with a higher Priority than the default player scripts' context and with Sink = true. Inputs bound in the Menu context are then consumed there and don't reach lower-priority contexts, like the default character controls that use IAS. You can also disable the gameplay context while the menu is open. Re-disable the menu context, or lower its priority, when it closes.

prompt: What is Roblox's CSS-like UI styling system? Name the main instances and explain how styles reach the UI and how a value is shared via tokens.
answer_key: Instances: StyleSheet (rules, tokens, themes), StyleRule (Selector + SetProperties), StyleLink (links a StyleSheet to a ScreenGui and its descendants), StyleDerive (inherit another sheet's tokens/themes)
Selectors can match class, tag (CollectionService), name, UI modifiers (e.g. UICorner), GuiState (e.g. Hover), and queries with '@'
Tokens are attributes on a token StyleSheet referenced with a '$' prefix (e.g. '$FrameColor'); themes are sets of tokens; only one StyleSheet applies to a given tree

responses.R1:
Roblox's engine UI styling (similar to CSS):
- StyleSheet: holds StyleRules (and token attributes).
- StyleRule: a Selector plus property overrides set with StyleRule:SetProperties({...}); rules can nest. Selectors match class names (Frame, TextButton), tags (".Tag" via CollectionService), instance names ("#Name"), state pseudo-classes (":hover" etc. via GuiState), phantom children like UICorner/UIStroke added by the rule ("::UICorner"), and queries prefixed @.
- StyleLink: links a StyleSheet to a ScreenGui (or other UI root) so its rules apply to that tree (one sheet per tree).
- StyleDerive: makes one sheet inherit another (e.g. a theme/token sheet).
- StyleQuery: conditional rules (MaxSize, PreferredInput, accessibility), e.g. @ViewportDisplaySizeSmall, @PreferredInputTouch.
- Studio Style Editor (beta) edits this visually.
How styles reach UI: a StyleLink under the ScreenGui points at the sheet; the engine matches rules' selectors against instances in that tree and applies the property overrides (higher-priority/more specific rules win), live as instances change.
Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (e.g. tokens:SetAttribute("Primary", Color3...)); derive it into the main sheet with StyleDerive; rules reference the token as a string "$Primary" (BackgroundColor3 = "$Primary"). Swapping the token sheet (themes with same token names) restyles everything. (UI Design Systems)
responses.R2:
It is the UI Styling system (Studio's CSS-like styles for GuiObjects).
Main instances:
- StyleSheet: a container of rules, like a CSS file. Holds StyleRules and tokens (attributes).
- StyleRule: has a Selector string (class name such as "TextButton", tag ".Primary", name "#Title", state ":Hover", and descendant/child combinators) and property values set with SetProperty/SetProperties. Rules have a Priority, and nested StyleRules work like nested CSS.
- StyleLink: placed inside a ScreenGui or other UI root (or the DataModel). Its StyleSheet property points at a StyleSheet, which applies it to that UI tree.
- StyleDerive: lets one StyleSheet inherit or extend another (themes).
How styles reach UI: a StyleLink under a LayerCollector applies the linked sheet. Each GuiObject whose class, tags (CollectionService tags, written with a "." prefix in selectors) or name match a rule's Selector gets the rule's properties. A property set directly on an instance overrides the style. More specific or higher-priority rules win.
Tokens: define attributes on the StyleSheet (for example PrimaryColor = Color3, CornerRadius = UDim) and reference them in rule values with "$PrimaryColor". Changing the token changes every rule that uses it. Swapping in a derived sheet with different token values gives theming such as dark and light.
responses.R3: Roblox's UI Styling system is a CSS-like set of instances. StyleSheet holds the rules and tokens. StyleRule has a Selector (class name, .tag, #name, :state like :hover, descendant/child combinators) and property values set via SetProperty/SetProperties, plus a Priority. StyleDerive makes one sheet inherit rules from another (themes, base sheets). StyleLink is placed in a ScreenGui (or other UI root) and points at a StyleSheet, applying it to that UI tree. StyleQuery adds conditional rules (screen size, aspect ratio, input type). Styles reach the UI because a StyleLink connects the sheet to a UI tree, and its rules then match GuiObjects by class, tag (CollectionService or the styling tags) or name, the way CSS does. Rule priority and specificity resolve conflicts, and properties set directly on an instance override styles. Tokens: define attributes on a (token) StyleSheet, for example PrimaryColor = Color3, and reference them in rule values as "$PrimaryColor". Swapping or deriving token sheets changes the theme everywhere. The Studio Style Editor is still in beta, and the selector syntax may change.
